plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It combines creative freedom with concrete completion criteria. The source, required engine, controller-first philosophy, attract mode, developer tools, and testing expectations make it possible to direct a distinctive game and define what a finished demo means. Leaving title selection to each builder also preserves a useful piece of creative ownership.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: The standalone multiplayer requirement does not specify whether couch co-op is sufficient or remote connectivity is mandatory. The required Hub client only provides embedded-session transport, not standalone signalling or matchmaking. The brief also leaves the intended campaign length and the practical boundary between a complete vertical slice and future designer tooling open to interpretation.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: The hardest part was reconciling source fidelity, a compact original campaign, single-file deployment, and genuinely working multiplayer without assuming nonexistent services. Research also mattered: the original ray destroys hostile swarms rather than freezing Beebots, and restoring twelve bees each wave is source-backed. Those details materially change the combat plan. No game was built or playtested during planning.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Specify the required standalone multiplayer modes and whether signalling or TURN infrastructure will be supplied. Give a preferred demo-duration range and a short definition of the expected designer tools. Centralize the delivery and attribution requirements in one checklist so the plan, in-game credits, chat feedback, and structured interview can be checked against the same source of truth.
